questions.passage:
Making market counts comparable

A group studying the use of a neighbourhood market wanted to know how many stalls were active at different times of day. Market records were kept mainly for collecting fees, and they sometimes included empty pitches that had already been paid for. To distinguish advertised capacity from activity, the researchers worked from direct observation.

Each observer carried a route card showing the order of the market lanes. Walking the same route on each visit meant that every lane was included. A stall counted as active if the visitor could see goods on display and a seller was present. The observers recorded shuttered pitches separately, since closing temporarily for deliveries was different from never opening.

At first, staff compared totals entered by different observers and found that some were counting portable racks as separate stalls. To deal with this inconsistency, the team took reference photographs of the most common ambiguous arrangements and discussed how each should count. Later pairs of observers were asked to make independent records before discussing any differences.

After the trial, the project team noticed that the final count could change simply because the last lane was usually reached when traders were beginning to pack away. They added a time stamp to the record for every lane so that comparisons could take that difference into account.

Notes: Consistency in market observations
- Follow the lane sequence on a [1] ___ to cover the entire site.
- Count a stall as active when a seller is present and [2] ___ can be seen.
- Use [3] ___ to help resolve inconsistent treatment of ambiguous layouts.
- Record a [4] ___ for each lane to account for changes during the walk.
questions.prompt:
Use no more than three words from the passage to complete this note.

- Follow the lane sequence on a [1] ___ to cover the entire site.
questions.explanation: The second paragraph identifies the route card as the guide to lane order.

questions.passage:
How an informal route becomes visible

A campus project on pedestrian movement began by looking for paths that had developed without formal planning. These paths often appeared as narrow lines across grass. For the first survey, volunteers drew the routes on base maps. They deliberately left out wider bare patches beside benches, which might have resulted from people standing rather than walking through.

The team then recorded when and how people used the routes. During fixed observation periods, volunteers noted the direction of travel, with particular attention to whether a path worked equally well in both directions. At a steep bank they saw that people often entered from above and returned along a longer paved route rather than climbing back up.

The path surfaces also changed with weather. After rain, a shallow puddle formed beside one entrance and some walkers moved around it. The project team identified a temporary branch in the worn line that was visible only after wet days. Treating that branch as a new permanent route would have overstated the effect of the rain.

When the results were discussed, one proposal was to surface every route that attracted users. The investigators advised a trial on the shortest clearly established link. Before any permanent work, they wanted to see whether a temporary surface would change movement at nearby entrances as well as on the path itself.

Notes: Evidence from informal campus routes
- Mark paths on [1] ___ but omit bare areas more consistent with standing still.
- To compare use in opposite directions, record the [2] ___.
- Avoid treating a [3] ___ that appears after rain as a permanent route.
- Trial a [4] ___ before deciding whether to install a permanent one.
questions.prompt:
Use no more than three words from the passage to complete this note.

- Mark paths on [1] ___ but omit bare areas more consistent with standing still.
questions.explanation: The first paragraph explains that volunteers drew routes on base maps.
